screens.title: Data Stores and Leaderboards: Persistent Player Data
screens.narratorSegment: Persistent data is what lets a player's progress survive between play sessions. In this chapter you'll see how Roblox's Data Stores provide server-side storage for per-player values like coins, inventory, and achievements, and how OrderedDataStores enable ranked leaderboards. We'll focus on the core service, safe operations, and a small, testable workflow that loads a player's coins when they join, updates them while they play, and writes them back on leave. You'll also learn the safer update pattern that reduces race conditions, why pcall is essential when calling Data Store functions, and how to use an OrderedDataStore to produce a top-ten UI. This matters because without reliable save and load mechanics, player progression is lost and retention drops. A concrete example you'll follow is a coin system: load coins on join, use UpdateAsync to increment safely when the player earns coins, and push their final total to an ordered leaderboard on exit. As you go through the lesson, watch for common mistakes like not handling nil returns, failing to enable A P I Services, or saving client-side data directly. By the end you'll understand how to persist player state securely and present a stable leaderboard.

screens.title: What are Data Stores?
screens.narratorSegment: Data Stores are Roblox's server-side storage for player-specific information that must persist across sessions. In practice this means coins, inventory, settings, and achievements live beyond a single play session and can be reliably retrieved later. A concrete example: a player's coin total is saved to a named Data Store using the player's UserId as a key. When the player rejoins, GetAsync returns the stored coin value or nil if no prior save exists; the script then initializes the player's coins to that value or to a sensible default like zero. Data Stores matter because they separate transient in-game state from long-term progress; without them players would lose progress and replay value would drop. One misconception is treating client-side values as persistent — clients cannot write to server Data Stores directly, and saving must be done on the server. Another common confusion is about types: Data Stores accept numbers, strings, booleans, and tables; Roblox handles JSON encoding for tables. Takeaway: think of a Data Store as a server ledger that maps keys to saved values. Example scenario: on PlayerAdded call a load function to GetAsync the UserId key, set the player's Coins attribute, and default to zero when nil is returned. What value will you choose as your default when no saved data exists?

keyIdea.title: Data Stores defined
keyIdea.text: Server-side storage that maps keys to values, used to persist per-player progress across sessions.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.5 › What are Data Stores?
Definition
Data Stores hold persistent player-specific values on Roblox servers. They let you save coins, inventory, and preferences so players return to progress they expect.
Example: Coins

Save a player's coin total under a key like their UserId and load it on join; default to zero if none exists.

Why it matters

Persistent saves enable meaningful progression and fair competition on leaderboards.

Key Takeaway

Treat Data Stores as authoritative server storage for game state that must persist across sessions.

Concrete code example
-- Server-side: load player coins
local DataStoreService = game:GetService("DataStoreService")
local Players = game:GetService("Players")

local playerDataStore = DataStoreService:GetDataStore("PlayerCoinsData")

local function loadData(player)
  local success, savedCoins = pcall(function()
    return playerDataStore:GetAsync(player.UserId)
  end)

  if success then
    if savedCoins ~= nil then
      player:SetAttribute("Coins", savedCoins)
    else
      player:SetAttribute("Coins", 0)
    end
  else
    warn("Error loading data for " .. player.Name .. ": " .. savedCoins)
    player:SetAttribute("Coins", 0)
  end
end

Players.PlayerAdded:Connect(loadData)
Common mistake

Relying on client saves or not handling nil from GetAsync for new players.

Pro tip

Always choose a clear default (e.g., 0 coins) so new players have consistent behavior.

screens.title: GetAsync and SetAsync: loading and saving
screens.narratorSegment: GetAsync and SetAsync are the basic Data Store operations to read and write values. GetAsync accepts a key, typically the player's UserId, and returns saved data or nil if none exists. SetAsync writes a value to the store under a key; the value can be a number, string, boolean or a table. Because these are network operations, always wrap them in pcall to catch failures. A practical flow is: on PlayerAdded call GetAsync in a pcall, set a default when nil is returned, and on PlayerRemoving call SetAsync in a pcall to persist the final in-game attribute. A concrete example in the chapter loads coins at join and saves them when the player leaves, printing success or warning on failure. A common misconception is assuming SetAsync will never fail; network issues and rate limits can cause errors. If a save fails, log the error and consider retrying on a short timer or queueing the data. Check your Game Settings to ensure A P I Services are enabled so these calls function in Studio. As a closing question: if SetAsync fails during PlayerRemoving, what fallback will you implement to avoid silent data loss?

keyIdea.text: Wrap GetAsync and SetAsync in pcall, handle nil results, and choose a fallback or retry strategy when saves fail.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.5 › GetAsync & SetAsync
Walkthrough: load and save

Follow this server-side pattern: pcall(GetAsync) on join, set defaults if nil, pcall(SetAsync) on leave. Always log failures.

-- Save and load pattern
local DataStoreService = game:GetService("DataStoreService")
local Players = game:GetService("Players")
local playerDataStore = DataStoreService:GetDataStore("PlayerCoinsData")

local function saveData(player)
  local success, err = pcall(function()
    playerDataStore:SetAsync(player.UserId, player:GetAttribute("Coins"))
  end)
  if success then
    print("Data saved for " .. player.Name .. ". Coins: " .. player:GetAttribute("Coins"))
  else
    warn("Error saving data for " .. player.Name .. ": " .. err)
  end
end

local function loadData(player)
  local success, savedCoins = pcall(function()
    return playerDataStore:GetAsync(player.UserId)
  end)

  if success then
    if savedCoins ~= nil then
      player:SetAttribute("Coins", savedCoins)
    else
      player:SetAttribute("Coins", 0)
    end
  else
    warn("Error loading data for " .. player.Name .. ": " .. savedCoins)
    player:SetAttribute("Coins", 0)
  end
end

Players.PlayerAdded:Connect(loadData)
Players.PlayerRemoving:Connect(saveData)
Example

Load coins with GetAsync on PlayerAdded, save with SetAsync on PlayerRemoving as shown above.

Misconception

Don't assume SetAsync never fails; handle errors and consider queuing or retrying.

Checklist
  • Wrap GetAsync/SetAsync in pcall
  • Handle nil returns for new players
  • Validate values before saving
Key Takeaway

Always protect Data Store calls with pcall and plan a fallback when network saves fail.

screens.title: UpdateAsync: safe concurrent updates
screens.narratorSegment: UpdateAsync is a robust method for modifying stored values because it asks you to provide a transform function. That transform function receives the current stored value and returns the new value. This pattern allows Roblox to retry the transform if simultaneous updates conflict, which reduces race conditions that occur when multiple servers try to write to the same key. For example, to increment a player's coins you provide a function that takes oldCoins, defaults it to zero when nil, and returns oldCoins plus the earned amount. The chapter's example shows using UpdateAsync in a pcall and then applying the returned new total to the player's in-game attribute. A common mistake is trying to read, modify, and SetAsync in separate steps — that opens a window for race conditions. Another misconception is thinking UpdateAsync always guarantees the last writer wins; it guarantees atomic application of your transform while managing retries, which makes merges safer. Takeaway: when changing numeric counters or merging tables, use UpdateAsync to keep server updates consistent. How would you design a transform function for adding items to a collection stored as a table?

keyIdea.title: Atomic updates with UpdateAsync
keyIdea.text: Provide a transform function to apply changes atomically and reduce race conditions across servers.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.5 › UpdateAsync
Process: increment safely
  1. Call UpdateAsync with the player key and a transformFunction.
  2. The transformFunction receives old value (or nil) and returns the new value.
  3. UpdateAsync applies the transform atomically and returns the final stored value.
  4. Update player's in-game attribute with the returned new value.
-- Using UpdateAsync to add coins
local function addCoins(player, amount)
  local success, newCoins = pcall(function()
    return playerDataStore:UpdateAsync(player.UserId, function(oldCoins)
      oldCoins = oldCoins or 0
      return oldCoins + amount
    end)
  end)

  if success then
    player:SetAttribute("Coins", newCoins)
    print(player.Name .. " gained " .. amount .. " coins. New total: " .. newCoins)
  else
    warn("Error updating coins for " .. player.Name .. ": " .. newCoins)
  end
end
Misconception

Don't read-modify-write outside UpdateAsync; that pattern is vulnerable to race conditions.

Analogy

Think of UpdateAsync as asking the server to open, modify, and safely close the value for you atomically.

Example scenario

Player picks up coins on multiple servers or during handoffs. Use UpdateAsync so each increment merges correctly into the stored total.

Key Takeaway

Use UpdateAsync with a transform function when changing counters or merging stored tables to avoid overwriting concurrent changes.

screens.title: pcall vs direct calls
screens.narratorSegment: pcall performs protected calls so a failing network request doesn't crash your entire server script. When interacting with Data Stores, you always want to use pcall around GetAsync, SetAsync, and UpdateAsync because these calls are remote requests to Roblox servers and can fail from network issues, rate limits, or outages. The chapter shows many examples wrapped in pcall: when success is true you use the returned data; when false you log a warning and apply a fallback. A concrete example: when GetAsync fails, set the player's coins to zero as a safe fallback and allow the player to continue playing rather than disconnecting or throwing an error. A misconception is that pcall hides errors; it doesn't — it captures them so you can decide what to do. Best practice is to log the error, consider exponential backoff retries for transient failures, and avoid retry storms that hit rate limits. In the context of leaderboards, catch errors on GetSortedAsync and return an empty table to the client so the UI can handle it gracefully. Closing question: what logging or retry strategy will you implement when a Data Store call returns an error?

keyIdea.text: pcall prevents script crashes and lets you handle Data Store errors with fallbacks, logs, and retries.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.5 › pcall vs direct calls
Direct call (unsafe)

Calling GetAsync or SetAsync without pcall can throw errors that stop your script. Avoid this in server-side persistence code.

When it fails

Network errors, rate limits, or Roblox service outages can cause failures; pcall lets you catch these.

Protected call (recommended)

Wrap calls in pcall, check success, log errors, and apply fallbacks like defaults or retries.

local success, result = pcall(function()
  return playerDataStore:GetAsync(player.UserId)
end)
if success then
  -- use result
else
  warn("Error loading data: " .. tostring(result))
  -- fallback
end
Pro tip

Avoid aggressive automatic retries that could trigger rate limits; instead, log and retry with backoff when appropriate.

screens.title: OrderedDataStore and leaderboards
screens.narratorSegment: OrderedDataStore is a special Data Store optimized for numeric rankings, which makes it ideal for leaderboards. Use GetOrderedDataStore with a unique name to obtain it, and then SetAsync to store non-negative integer scores for each player's key. To show a Top 10, call GetSortedAsync with descending order and a page size, then retrieve the current page from the returned DataStorePages object. The chapter gives a practical example: when a player leaves, update their final coin count to the OrderedDataStore using SetAsync, and on a periodic server job call GetSortedAsync to fetch the top entries. A misconception is attempting to store complex tables in an OrderedDataStore; OrderedDataStore values must be numeric for ranking. When you fetch pages, iterate the page entries, map user IDs to names using Players:GetNameFromUserIdAsync, and package rank, name, and score for clients. If GetSortedAsync fails inside pcall, return an empty list so the UI can show a graceful message. Takeaway question: how will you handle ties in scores when presenting ranks in the UI? content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.5 › OrderedDataStore
How it fits together
Use OrderedDataStore for numeric rankings. Update player scores on leave and periodically fetch sorted pages to display a Top N list.
local leaderboardStore = DataStoreService:GetOrderedDataStore("TopCoinEarners")

local function updateLeaderboard(player, score)
  local success, err = pcall(function()
    leaderboardStore:SetAsync(player.UserId, score)
  end)
  if not success then
    warn("Error updating leaderboard for " .. player.Name .. ": " .. err)
  end
end

-- Display top players
local function displayLeaderboard()
  local success, pages = pcall(function()
    return leaderboardStore:GetSortedAsync(false, 10)
  end)

  if success then
    local topPlayers = pages:GetCurrentPage()
    for rank, entry in ipairs(topPlayers) do
      local userId = entry.key
      local score = entry.value
      local playerName = Players:GetNameFromUserIdAsync(userId) or "Unknown Player"
      print(rank .. ". " .. playerName .. ": " .. score .. " coins")
    end
  else
    warn("Error getting leaderboard data: " .. pages)
  end
end
Key Takeaway

OrderedDataStore stores numerical scores for ranking; use GetSortedAsync to fetch ordered pages safely.

UI considerations

Map user IDs to display names on the server, return compact tables to clients, and have the client render ranks in a ScreenGui.

Tip

Keep leaderboard updates batched and infrequent to reduce Data Store requests and respect rate limits.

Common mistake

Storing non-numeric values in an OrderedDataStore—ranked values must be numeric integers.

Module 5 › Chapter 5.5 › PlayerDataHandler
Server script (continued)
-- ServerScriptService/PlayerDataHandler
local DataStoreService = game:GetService("DataStoreService")
local Players = game:GetService("Players")
local ReplicatedStorage = game:GetService("ReplicatedStorage")

local playerDataStore = DataStoreService:GetDataStore("PlayerCoinsData")
local leaderboardStore = DataStoreService:GetOrderedDataStore("TopCoinEarners")

local getLeaderboardData = Instance.new("RemoteFunction")
getLeaderboardData.Name = "GetLeaderboardData"
getLeaderboardData.Parent = ReplicatedStorage

local function saveData(player)
  local success, err = pcall(function()
    playerDataStore:SetAsync(player.UserId, player:GetAttribute("Coins"))
  end)
  if not success then
    warn("Error saving data for " .. player.Name .. ": " .. err)
  end
end

local function updateLeaderboard(player, score)
  local success, err = pcall(function()
    leaderboardStore:SetAsync(player.UserId, score)
  end)
  if not success then
    warn("Error updating leaderboard for " .. player.Name .. ": " .. err)
  end
end

Players.PlayerRemoving:Connect(function(player)
  local coins = player:GetAttribute("Coins") or 0
  updateLeaderboard(player, coins)
  saveData(player)
end)
Key Takeaway

A single server script can manage saves, leaderboard pushes, and a remote function for client requests.

  • Enable API Services in Game Settings
  • Run multiple Play sessions in Studio to simulate concurrent updates
  • Verify PlayerAdded sets attribute and PlayerRemoving saves and updates leaderboard
Common improvement

Add periodic auto-saves during play to protect against crashes that skip PlayerRemoving.

Module 5 › Chapter 5.5 › Client-server leaderboard
Server: OnServerInvoke handler
getLeaderboardData.OnServerInvoke = function(player)
  local success, pages = pcall(function()
    return leaderboardStore:GetSortedAsync(false, 10)
  end)

  if success then
    local topPlayers = pages:GetCurrentPage()
    local leaderboardTable = {}
    for rank, entry in ipairs(topPlayers) do
      local userId = entry.key
      local score = entry.value
      local playerName = Players:GetNameFromUserIdAsync(userId)
      table.insert(leaderboardTable, {Rank = rank, Name = playerName, Score = score})
    end
    return leaderboardTable
  else
    warn("Error getting leaderboard data for " .. player.Name .. ": " .. pages)
    return {}
  end
end
Client: LocalScript summary

Invoke the server periodically, clear existing UI entries, and create a TextLabel per returned row showing rank, name, and score.

UI behavior & rate limits
  • Request leaderboard data every 15–30 seconds to avoid excessive Data Store calls.
  • Show a placeholder or message when the server returns an empty table.
  • Keep client rendering lightweight—server should resolve names and pack the data.
Key Takeaway

Server mediates Data Store access; clients request compact, ready-to-render leaderboard tables via RemoteFunction.

fullNarratorScript:
Persistent data is what lets a player's progress survive between play sessions. In this chapter you'll see how Roblox's Data Stores provide server-side storage for per-player values like coins, inventory, and achievements, and how OrderedDataStores enable ranked leaderboards. We'll focus on the core service, safe operations, and a small, testable workflow that loads a player's coins when they join, updates them while they play, and writes them back on leave. You'll also learn the safer update pattern that reduces race conditions, why pcall is essential when calling Data Store functions, and how to use an OrderedDataStore to produce a top-ten UI. This matters because without reliable save and load mechanics, player progression is lost and retention drops. A concrete example you'll follow is a coin system: load coins on join, use UpdateAsync to increment safely when the player earns coins, and push their final total to an ordered leaderboard on exit. As you go through the lesson, watch for common mistakes like not handling nil returns, failing to enable A P I Services, or saving client-side data directly. By the end you'll understand how to persist player state securely and present a stable leaderboard.

By the end of the first objectives block you'll be able to identify what Data Stores do and how to use the main DataStoreService methods. You will learn to get a named data store and call GetAsync to load data tied to a player key. You will also practice saving with SetAsync and discover why UpdateAsync is the safer choice for concurrent updates. Each objective includes a brief rationale so you understand where and why to use these calls in your game flow. For example, loading a player's coin total with GetAsync at join keeps progress intact; saving that total with SetAsync on leaving persists it across sessions. A frequent misconception is thinking SetAsync automatically solves concurrency; UpdateAsync actually reduces race conditions by applying a transform function to current stored data. These skills matter because they directly impact player retention and fairness. Finally, you'll verify competency with a milestone that asks you to implement a basic load/save cycle using DataStoreService and pcall error handling.

This second objectives block focuses on leaderboards, safe network calls, and operational concerns. You'll implement an OrderedDataStore to keep ranked numeric values suitable for leaderboards and use GetSortedAsync to fetch top entries with pagination. You will also learn to wrap every Data Store call in pcall so that transient errors don't crash your server; instead you can warn, retry, or fall back to defaults. Another objective is to design a simple client-server flow: the server provides leaderboard data through a RemoteFunction and the client renders it in a ScreenGui. Finally, you will learn operational practices: enable A P I Services in Game Settings, avoid excessive requests to respect rate limits, and validate any data before saving. A concrete example is updating a player's final coin total to an OrderedDataStore on PlayerRemoving, then periodically calling GetSortedAsync on the server and returning the top entries to clients. Understanding these steps prevents lost progress and ensures a fair, stable leaderboard experience for players.

Data Stores are Roblox's server-side storage for player-specific information that must persist across sessions. In practice this means coins, inventory, settings, and achievements live beyond a single play session and can be reliably retrieved later. A concrete example: a player's coin total is saved to a named Data Store using the player's UserId as a key. When the player rejoins, GetAsync returns the stored coin value or nil if no prior save exists; the script then initializes the player's coins to that value or to a sensible default like zero. Data Stores matter because they separate transient in-game state from long-term progress; without them players would lose progress and replay value would drop. One misconception is treating client-side values as persistent — clients cannot write to server Data Stores directly, and saving must be done on the server. Another common confusion is about types: Data Stores accept numbers, strings, booleans, and tables; Roblox handles JSON encoding for tables. Takeaway: think of a Data Store as a server ledger that maps keys to saved values. Example scenario: on PlayerAdded call a load function to GetAsync the UserId key, set the player's Coins attribute, and default to zero when nil is returned. What value will you choose as your default when no saved data exists?

GetAsync and SetAsync are the basic Data Store operations to read and write values. GetAsync accepts a key, typically the player's UserId, and returns saved data or nil if none exists. SetAsync writes a value to the store under a key; the value can be a number, string, boolean or a table. Because these are network operations, always wrap them in pcall to catch failures. A practical flow is: on PlayerAdded call GetAsync in a pcall, set a default when nil is returned, and on PlayerRemoving call SetAsync in a pcall to persist the final in-game attribute. A concrete example in the chapter loads coins at join and saves them when the player leaves, printing success or warning on failure. A common misconception is assuming SetAsync will never fail; network issues and rate limits can cause errors. If a save fails, log the error and consider retrying on a short timer or queueing the data. Check your Game Settings to ensure A P I Services are enabled so these calls function in Studio. As a closing question: if SetAsync fails during PlayerRemoving, what fallback will you implement to avoid silent data loss?

UpdateAsync is a robust method for modifying stored values because it asks you to provide a transform function. That transform function receives the current stored value and returns the new value. This pattern allows Roblox to retry the transform if simultaneous updates conflict, which reduces race conditions that occur when multiple servers try to write to the same key. For example, to increment a player's coins you provide a function that takes oldCoins, defaults it to zero when nil, and returns oldCoins plus the earned amount. The chapter's example shows using UpdateAsync in a pcall and then applying the returned new total to the player's in-game attribute. A common mistake is trying to read, modify, and SetAsync in separate steps — that opens a window for race conditions. Another misconception is thinking UpdateAsync always guarantees the last writer wins; it guarantees atomic application of your transform while managing retries, which makes merges safer. Takeaway: when changing numeric counters or merging tables, use UpdateAsync to keep server updates consistent. How would you design a transform function for adding items to a collection stored as a table?

pcall performs protected calls so a failing network request doesn't crash your entire server script. When interacting with Data Stores, you always want to use pcall around GetAsync, SetAsync, and UpdateAsync because these calls are remote requests to Roblox servers and can fail from network issues, rate limits, or outages. The chapter shows many examples wrapped in pcall: when success is true you use the returned data; when false you log a warning and apply a fallback. A concrete example: when GetAsync fails, set the player's coins to zero as a safe fallback and allow the player to continue playing rather than disconnecting or throwing an error. A misconception is that pcall hides errors; it doesn't — it captures them so you can decide what to do. Best practice is to log the error, consider exponential backoff retries for transient failures, and avoid retry storms that hit rate limits. In the context of leaderboards, catch errors on GetSortedAsync and return an empty table to the client so the UI can handle it gracefully. Closing question: what logging or retry strategy will you implement when a Data Store call returns an error?

OrderedDataStore is a special Data Store optimized for numeric rankings, which makes it ideal for leaderboards. Use GetOrderedDataStore with a unique name to obtain it, and then SetAsync to store non-negative integer scores for each player's key. To show a Top 10, call GetSortedAsync with descending order and a page size, then retrieve the current page from the returned DataStorePages object. The chapter gives a practical example: when a player leaves, update their final coin count to the OrderedDataStore using SetAsync, and on a periodic server job call GetSortedAsync to fetch the top entries. A misconception is attempting to store complex tables in an OrderedDataStore; OrderedDataStore values must be numeric for ranking. When you fetch pages, iterate the page entries, map user IDs to names using Players:GetNameFromUserIdAsync, and package rank, name, and score for clients. If GetSortedAsync fails inside pcall, return an empty list so the UI can show a graceful message. Takeaway question: how will you handle ties in scores when presenting ranks in the UI? OrderedDataStore and leaderboards means store numeric scores and use getsortedasync plus pages to retrieve ranked entries for display.. In practical terms, how to store and retrieve ranked scores for a top 10. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

A practical server-side script ties everything together: obtain DataStoreService, get your named Data Store, and implement load and save functions connected to PlayerAdded and PlayerRemoving. The chapter provides a tested example that creates a playerDataStore, loads coins on PlayerAdded using GetAsync inside pcall, and saves on PlayerRemoving using SetAsync inside pcall. These are the core terms you should remember from this chapter. Data Stores are the server-side mechanism for saving player-specific values across sessions. DataStoreService is the Roblox A P I that provides access to both standard Data Stores and OrderedDataStores. GetDataStore(name) returns a Data Store object for saving and loading arbitrary values under keys. Remember to use GetAsync to load a value and SetAsync to save, and prefer UpdateAsync when you need atomic modifications. Use pcall to wrap all Data Store operations, so your server can handle transient failures without crashing. OrderedDataStore is for numeric ranking, and GetSortedAsync returns pages you can iterate to build leaderboards. Keep rate limits in mind and enable A P I Services for Studio testing.
